# Coat collection for the winter cupboard

We are asking for washed, wearable coats rather than bags of unsorted clothing. Volunteers have room to hang coats immediately, but the cupboard has no laundry facilities and little space for sorting other garments. Ready-to-wear coats can reach households sooner.

Drop-off sessions will run on Wednesday from five until seven and Saturday from ten until twelve. Use the side entrance of the community hall, where a volunteer will count the coats and offer a receipt if you want one. The main hall is being used by the dance class during the Wednesday session.

Children's sizes are especially useful this year. Please fasten a paper note to the hanger with the size shown on the label. Where the label has faded, leave the size blank rather than guessing. Volunteers will measure those coats before putting them on the children's rail.

The collection is restricted to clean coats people can wear straight away because we cannot wash them or sort mixed clothing bags in the space available. That makes them quicker to pass on. We have borrowed extra hangers from the school, so donors can keep their own hangers if they need them.

The cupboard opens for collections on the following Monday. Households can visit without a referral, and the volunteer at the desk will help find a suitable size. The children's area has a mirror and a low bench so coats can be tried over ordinary school clothing.

If you want to donate money instead, ask the desk volunteer for the cupboard fund details. The fund pays for replacement zips fitted by the local repair group and for a small reserve of sizes that donations have not supplied. The treasurer will post a spending summary at the end of winter alongside the coat totals.

# A quieter hour at the pool

The pool's quiet-hour trial began in March with music switched off and announcements limited to urgent messages. The aim was to make a session usable for swimmers who found the ordinary background noise difficult. Staff also dimmed the reception display, which had been mentioned in the initial access survey.

The first four sessions attracted fewer swimmers than an ordinary Tuesday hour. However, nine people attended every week, including four who said they had previously stopped using the pool. Their comments pointed to the changing rooms as the remaining problem. The hand dryers there were louder than anything they encountered beside the water.

From next week, paper towels will be available in the smaller changing room during quiet hour, and its hand dryer will be switched off. The larger changing room will keep its usual equipment. Staff will explain the two routes at reception so people can choose without entering the noisier room first.

The original aim of reducing background noise now extends beyond the swimming session to the route through the building. That change follows the trial's comments: someone could manage the pool itself and still find arrival and changing difficult. The next feedback card will ask separately about those stages.

Quiet hour remains Tuesday from two until three. Book through the normal system or ask reception to make a booking. Companions who are helping a swimmer should tell reception when booking so staff can explain the changing-room arrangements in advance.

The trial will continue for another six weeks. The access group will review attendance alongside the separate arrival, changing, and swimming comments. Residents who have not tried the session can ask for a brief visit before booking; staff can show the route while the pool is being prepared.

# Before the street market opens

Stallholders can enter through the west barrier from seven until half past eight. Show the vehicle pass to the marshal, unload beside your numbered pitch, and move the vehicle to the school car park. The east barrier remains reserved for emergency access.

Each pitch has a number painted on the kerb. Put tables behind that number, leaving the marked pedestrian strip clear. The marshal has a copy of the pitch plan if a number has become obscured. Electricity is available only at pitches marked with a socket symbol; an extension lead does not turn an unpowered pitch into an approved powered one.

Food stalls need to display their inspection paperwork at the front of the stall. The market officer will visit before opening. Keep waste containers behind the table, and take trade waste away at the end of the day. The street bins are for visitors.

At half past eight, the marshal will close the west barrier to vehicles. Any vehicle still inside must leave before the barrier is secured. Trading begins at nine, after the market officer has checked the pedestrian route and emergency access.

Opening checklist

- Enter at the west barrier with your pass.
- Unload at your numbered pitch and move the vehicle to the school car park before half past eight.
- Put tables behind the kerb number and clear the pedestrian strip.
- Display food inspection paperwork where applicable.
- Place waste containers behind the table and retain trade waste for removal.
- Wait for the nine o'clock opening after the route check.

The marshal will be beside the west barrier during setup. If your allocated space is obstructed, speak to the marshal before unloading rather than moving to another pitch. A different pitch may have been assigned equipment or an electrical supply another stallholder needs.

# Evening classes: paying for materials

The pottery class fee includes tuition and use of the studio tools. Clay and firing are charged separately according to the work each student makes. This keeps a student making a few small pieces from paying the same materials amount as someone making large pots.

Enrolment opens at the arts centre desk on Monday. The course runs for eight Thursday evenings, with a break during half-term. Beginners and returning students are welcome. Bring an apron and a small notebook; the studio provides the basic hand tools and has a limited number of aprons available to borrow.

The tutor will show students how to label their work before it goes onto the drying shelves. Put your initials and class number underneath each piece. A paper name card can become separated from a pot when work is moved, so the mark on the piece itself is important.

Materials are billed against what an individual makes rather than shared equally across the class. A few small items therefore attract a different materials cost from several large pots. The desk will accept those payments by card, and receipts can be collected at the following session if the printer is unavailable.

The first evening includes a demonstration of the studio's glazing samples. Students can choose a finish from the fired sample board before buying glaze for a project. The tutor will explain which finishes suit the clay supplied and how the firing schedule affects collection dates.

Finished work can be collected during desk hours after the tutor confirms it is ready. Bring your receipt or class card so staff can identify the right shelf. If you cannot collect before the next course begins, tell the desk so your pieces can be boxed and labelled rather than left among work awaiting its first firing.

# Three places to get help with forms

The advice service will use three venues while its office heating is replaced. Each venue offers a different part of the service, so check the arrangement before travelling. Appointments already booked at the office will be moved by staff, who will contact the people concerned directly.

For housing forms, go to the library meeting room on Tuesday mornings. The adviser there can help identify required documents and complete the application with you. Bring the letter giving your application reference and any documents named in it. The library desk can show you the room but cannot access your case.

For benefits forms, go to the health centre's community room on Wednesday afternoons. The adviser can help with the form and explain how to supply supporting evidence. Bring the current form or the message asking for an update. Appointments need to be booked through the advice service because the health centre reception team does not hold the list.

For scanning and uploading documents, go to the council hub on Friday mornings. A volunteer can help use the scanner and check that the upload confirmation has appeared. Bring the documents and the reference for the application receiving them. The volunteer will ask you to enter any account password yourself.

Someone completing a housing form may therefore need both the Tuesday adviser and the Friday scanning session. The first appointment deals with what the application says; the second handles sending documents that the application requires. Ask the adviser to write the upload destination on your appointment slip if you need that second visit.

The telephone number remains the same throughout the move. Leave a message with your name and a callback number if staff are with another caller. The recorded greeting will give the current venues and the expected date for returning to the office.

# Community garden seed orders

The garden committee recommends keeping one combined seed order this spring. Buying together reaches the supplier's free-delivery threshold, while separate small orders would each attract postage. The saving can go toward replacement labels and trays.

Order sheets will be available in the greenhouse from Saturday. Write the crop, variety, packet size, and quantity you want. The supplier offers two similarly named climbing beans, so copy the catalogue code as well as the name. A catalogue is attached to the greenhouse shelf with string to keep it available for everyone.

Payments should go in the locked box beside the shed. Put your name and order total on the envelope, and keep a note of the amount. The treasurer will check payments against the sheets on Wednesday before placing the order. If a variety has sold out, she will contact the person ordering it rather than accept a substitute automatically.

The communal beds need separate attention. Their seed list is already approved and will be entered by the gardening coordinator. Individual plot holders should leave those rows blank, even when they have volunteered to sow a communal crop. The coordinator will assign the packets when they arrive.

A single order remains the sensible option because it avoids the postage attached to individual orders and qualifies for free delivery. Labels and trays can be bought with the money saved. The supplier has agreed to pack the communal-bed seeds in a separate bag, which should make sorting the delivery quicker.

Collection will be at the shed on the Saturday after delivery. Check your packets against your copy of the order before leaving. If you cannot attend, nominate another plot holder on the sheet so the coordinator can record who took the packets and avoid setting them aside a second time.

# Comparing two admission rates

A department's admission rate divides its offers by its applications. The university rate combines the offers and applications from every department. These rates answer different questions because departments receive different numbers of applications.

Consider a small illustration. Department A offers places to 80 of 100 applicants in one group and 9 of 10 in another. Department B offers places to 1 of 10 in the first group and 20 of 100 in the second. Within each department the second group has the higher admission rate. Across the university, however, the first group receives 81 offers from 110 applications, while the second receives 29 from 110.

The reversal occurs because the groups applied in different proportions to the two departments. Most applicants in the first group selected the department with the higher overall acceptance rate. Combining the departments changes the comparison by giving each group's departmental rates different weights. The university totals remain arithmetically correct.

For an admissions inquiry, the next question is substantive. Did applicants have similar preparation? Were they steered towards particular departments? Did a department change its available places? Department-level comparisons remove one source of aggregation, but those questions require additional records.

Use this order when presenting the figures:

- Show offers and applications together for each department and group.
- Compare rates within departments.
- Show how applications are distributed across departments before giving the combined rates.

This sequence lets readers see both the local comparisons and the weights behind the university total. A university-wide rate describes the outcome of the whole application process; a departmental rate describes outcomes conditional on applying there. Choosing between them depends on which part of that process the inquiry addresses.

Students selected for extra tuition because of one unusually low test result will often score higher on a second test. An unusually low result can combine a student's usual performance with a bad day. On the next test, that temporary disadvantage may be absent, so the result can rise even if the student's underlying proficiency has not changed.

The timing of the tests matters for other reasons too. If the second assessment covers material taught during the intervening month, ordinary classroom instruction could contribute to an increase. If it reuses the same questions, remembering particular answers could help. A report should describe both the interval and whether the forms were reused.

A later improvement can reflect the disappearance of the temporary factors that helped produce the low initial score, rather than any increase in underlying proficiency. This tendency is called regression toward the mean.

To estimate the tuition programme's contribution, eligible students could be allocated by lottery to an immediate start or a delayed start. Both groups would take the same assessment at the same time. The comparison would then address a difference in improvement between groups facing the same calendar and testing conditions. Attendance should also be recorded, since an offer of tuition and actual attendance answer different evaluation questions.

The assessment report needs to give the selection rule, the number of eligible students, and the number with results at both time points. It should describe any departures from the lottery and explain how missing follow-up results were handled. The initial result may have been depressed by an unusually bad day, and the following result can improve simply because that temporary influence is gone. A table of group sizes beside the estimated difference will help readers judge the scale of the comparison.

## Reading an incomplete passenger list

A missing name in a surviving passenger list can mean that the person did not travel, but it can also mean that the relevant page was lost. Absence from the surviving document therefore leaves those two possibilities open. The physical condition of the source belongs in the historical argument.

The register used in this exercise begins halfway through a numbered page. Three leaves have been cut out near the binding, and a later clerk has added totals on the inside cover. Students should describe those features before extracting names. A total copied onto the cover might refer to the original volume rather than the pages now present.

Handwriting creates another difficulty. The clerk sometimes abbreviated given names and occasionally put a place of residence in the space normally used for a surname. Compare repeated letter shapes within the same hand before deciding that an unfamiliar mark is a different initial. Record a doubtful reading with an uncertainty marker rather than silently choosing the most familiar name.

The transcription should preserve page numbers and indicate where a line continues from a missing page. Someone absent from the surviving list may either have stayed behind or appeared on a page that has since disappeared. Keep expansions of abbreviations in a separate column so another reader can recover the clerk's actual wording.

For the final exercise, select one named passenger and seek a second record made for a different purpose, such as a port payment or a household letter. Compare the dates and identifying details before treating the records as the same person. Submit the transcription together with a short account of the link you accepted and the evidence that made it persuasive.

documents.text:
# What 'some' contributes

In ordinary conversation, saying that some students passed often suggests that others failed. In a simple logical analysis, however, 'some students passed' requires at least one student to have passed and is compatible with everyone passing. The suggested limit and the minimum asserted content need to be distinguished.

Imagine a tutor who knows all the results and is asked whether the whole class passed. If she replies, 'Some students passed,' a listener may reason that she would have given the stronger answer if she could. The impression that some failed comes partly from the question and the tutor's apparent knowledge.

Change the situation. A visiting lecturer has marked only five papers from a class of thirty and says, 'Some students passed; I haven't seen the remaining papers.' The second clause makes the limit on her knowledge explicit. Her first clause now offers the result she can support while leaving the unmarked papers open.

A useful classroom exercise is to compare that sentence with 'Some students passed, in fact everyone did.' The continuation may sound like a correction of an expectation, but it need not contradict the first clause's minimum claim. Students should identify which expectation changes and which assertion remains satisfied.

## Testing the interpretation

Work in pairs with one person supplying the question and the other reading the answer. On the first round, ask whether anyone passed. On the second, ask whether everyone passed. Keep the answer itself unchanged and write down whether it feels sufficient in each exchange. A difference in how complete the answer feels gives us evidence about the role of the question, even before we decide how to describe the inference formally.

Then add a brief account of the speaker's access to the marks. One version can make the speaker the examination officer; another can make the speaker a student who has spoken with three friends. Compare the interpretations again. Record the exact dialogue rather than only your final judgment, since another pair needs the context to assess your reasoning.

For analysis, write down three things separately: the words used, the question being answered, and what the speaker is presented as knowing. Then test a continuation that withdraws the suggested limit. This helps locate the source of the interpretation. In a report of examination outcomes, an exact count usually avoids the ambiguity altogether; in a dialogue exercise, keeping the same word across changed contexts lets us examine how the inference is produced.

documents.text:
# Pooling samples in the meadow exercise

Pooling samples from several plots gives one combined measurement. It hides variation between plots because the laboratory receives their contents together. A very abundant species can dominate that combined result, leaving a rare species with little influence on the average.

## Collection

In the meadow exercise, teams should collect from the marked corners rather than choosing the greenest patch. Place the plot code on the bag before taking the sample. The code identifies the location even if the contents later dry to an indistinguishable mixture. Record the collection time and whether the ground was wet.

## Laboratory preparation

Drying conditions need to be consistent across teams. Use the assigned trays, retain the bag labels beside them, and weigh only after the scheduled drying period. Combining the plots removes the separate plot measurements, so differences between locations disappear inside the pooled sample. Trays should be cleaned between batches because loose fragments can remain in their corners.

## Reporting

The class spreadsheet has separate fields for fresh mass and dry mass. Enter the unit in the column heading and use the same balance throughout a batch. If a balance is replaced during the session, record the change beside the affected rows. Photograph any label whose writing has become difficult to read before copying its code.

The common species will still account for most of the combined average, while the scarce one contributes relatively little. Each team should upload its field sheet alongside the measurements by the end of the session. The demonstrator will check that bag codes match the spreadsheet before the samples are cleared from the benches. Keep the original field sheets until that check is complete.

## Choosing a measure of typical rent

For a description of what a household near the middle of the local rental market pays, the median is the more useful starting point. It places half the observed rents on either side of a central position. The mean instead divides total rent by the number of properties.

Consider five monthly rents: 600, 650, 700, 750, and 2,300. The median is 700, while the mean is 1,000. The expensive property affects the mean strongly because its full value enters the total. The median depends on its position above the middle rather than how far above the middle it lies.

That feature also limits the median. If the most expensive property rises from 2,300 to 3,300, the median stays at 700 although aggregate rent increases. Use the recorded interview rather than the recollection written a week later when quoting the participant. The recording preserves the participant's wording; the later account may substitute the researcher's phrasing. In the methods exercise, both files are available so students can see how their purposes differ.

The recollection contains useful observations that the microphone could not capture. It notes where the participant pointed, when a colleague entered the room, and which diagram was lying on the table. Keep those observations attributed to the researcher. They may clarify a reference such as 'that route' when the spoken words alone leave its object uncertain.

Transcription should retain a timestamp at each change of speaker. Long pauses can be marked where they affect the interpretation, but the exercise does not require measuring every silence. Use one consistent convention for words obscured by traffic noise, and preserve a link to the relevant section of audio so another student can listen.

The class copy uses the study code in both the transcript and the field notes, which allows comparison without displaying the participant's address. For quotations, the recorded interview remains the right source because it retains the participant's words instead of the researcher's later reconstruction.

Submit a short transcript extract with the timestamp and a note explaining any gesture needed to interpret it. If the gesture is described only in the field notes, identify that source explicitly. The exercise will be discussed in pairs before the final transcript is added to the shared study folder.

# Inspecting the fitted line

For these observations, a straight line is inadequate because the residuals rise at both ends and fall in the middle. The curve in the residual plot means that the line systematically misses part of the relationship, rather than scattering errors evenly around zero.

## Reading the axes

The horizontal axis shows fitted values and the vertical axis shows observed minus fitted values. A positive residual places the observation above the line. Students sometimes reverse that subtraction and then describe the pattern backwards, so state the convention before interpreting the figure. The units on the vertical axis remain the units of the measured response.

The measurements come from repeated heating runs on labelled vessels. A vessel code identifies the physical object, while a run code identifies a particular occasion on which it was measured. Keep both columns in the working file. Combining them into a single label would make it harder to distinguish variation between vessels from variation across runs on the same vessel. The laboratory sheet also records which thermometer was used, allowing an apparent batch difference to be checked against an instrument change.

## Checking the records

Two observations near the upper end have large residuals. Check their original worksheets for transcription errors before choosing a different model. A correct extreme observation belongs in the analysis; an entry copied into the wrong unit should be corrected and documented. The spreadsheet retains both the original entry and the correction in separate columns. A straight line is therefore inadequate for these observations.

## Planning the next fit

A curved fit should be motivated by the measurement process and checked against observations throughout the range. Adding enough terms can follow the data closely while behaving poorly between measured points. Reserve part of a sufficiently large dataset for checking predictive performance, keeping repeated measurements from the same object together when splitting.

For this exercise, submit the residual plot, the record checks for the two large residuals, and one proposed alternative form with a reason tied to the experiment. Include the range over which you would use that alternative. The next class will compare the proposals before any final model is selected.

documents.text:
A rate compares a quantity with an exposure. Dividing the number of bus breakdowns by kilometres travelled gives breakdowns per kilometre. It expresses failures relative to how far the buses ran.

Suppose one depot records twenty breakdowns over a million kilometres and another records fifteen over half a million. The second depot has fewer recorded breakdowns but a higher rate: thirty per million kilometres compared with twenty. The exposure changes the comparison because the depots did different amounts of driving.

The denominator still needs a suitable definition. Passenger kilometres would answer a question about service experienced by passengers, giving a crowded bus more weight than an empty one. Vehicle kilometres answer a question about fleet operation. Neither can be selected solely because it produces a smaller number. The report should identify the operational question before choosing the rate.

Reporting per million kilometres makes the values easier to read than small decimal fractions per kilometre. It changes the scale of presentation while preserving the ordering and ratio of the rates. A chart should keep that scaling consistent across depots and years; otherwise the labels can imply changes that arose only from a different multiplier.

Finally, record what counts as a breakdown. A fault fixed during a scheduled stop and a failure requiring a replacement bus could have different consequences. If the count includes both, a second measure of lost service minutes may help describe those consequences. The exercise is to prepare one comparison with the exposure, event definition, and display scale written alongside it, then explain the decision that comparison could inform.

Objects made from stone are more likely to survive in this soil than objects made from wood. The excavated collection can therefore overrepresent stone tools relative to the tools people actually used. Interpreting a display requires attention to the process that produced the surviving collection.

The teaching case contains material from three pits excavated in different years. The earliest excavation retained only complete implements, while the later teams also collected fragments. Counts across the three pits consequently reflect different collection practices as well as any differences in their contents. Students should inspect the excavation notes before treating each cabinet as a comparable sample.

Descriptions can preserve these distinctions economically. A label might state that the cabinet contains complete implements retained during the first excavation. Another can explain why the fragments from the later pits were kept: their broken edges may show manufacturing stages that a finished object conceals. Drawings of those edges let visitors follow the interpretation without handling the originals.

The photograph panel should include a scale and identify which surfaces have been reconstructed. Because wooden objects decay more readily here, stone objects have a better chance of reaching the excavation; the recovered tools can consequently make stone use appear more common than it was. A contrasting background will help visitors distinguish the pale fragments from the support material used to hold them upright.

For the assessed exercise, propose captions for one complete implement and one fragment. Each caption should distinguish what is physically present from the activity inferred from it. Add a source note pointing to the excavation record that supports the inference. The class will compare how much interpretation a short label can carry while keeping the evidence visible.

paragraphs.text: Objects made from stone are more likely to survive in this soil than objects made from wood. The excavated collection can therefore overrepresent stone tools relative to the tools people actually used. Interpreting a display requires attention to the process that produced the surviving collection.

The teaching case contains material from three pits excavated in different years. The earliest excavation retained only complete implements, while the later teams also collected fragments. Counts across the three pits consequently reflect different collection practices as well as any differences in their contents. Students should inspect the excavation notes before treating each cabinet as a comparable sample.

Descriptions can preserve these distinctions economically. A label might state that the cabinet contains complete implements retained during the first excavation. Another can explain why the fragments from the later pits were kept: their broken edges may show manufacturing stages that a finished object conceals. Drawings of those edges let visitors follow the interpretation without handling the originals.

The photograph panel should include a scale and identify which surfaces have been reconstructed. Because wooden objects decay more readily here, stone objects have a better chance of reaching the excavation; the recovered tools can consequently make stone use appear more common than it was. A contrasting background will help visitors distinguish the pale fragments from the support material used to hold them upright.

For the assessed exercise, propose captions for one complete implement and one fragment. Each caption should distinguish what is physically present from the activity inferred from it. Add a source note pointing to the excavation record that supports the inference. The class will compare how much interpretation a short label can carry while keeping the evidence visible.

## Why a queue can persist beside an empty desk

A service centre can have an empty desk and a waiting queue at the same time when the desk cannot handle the work in that queue. In our exercise, general enquiries and document checks require different staff permissions. Counting all open desks together hides that restriction.

At nine, three general-enquiry desks and one document-check desk open. General enquiries take about five minutes each, while document checks take fifteen. A clerk finishing a general enquiry may have spare time but still lack permission to certify a document. Sending a waiting applicant to that clerk would move the person without completing the service.

There are two possible changes to examine. Training a second clerk for document checks increases the capacity available to that queue. Moving a general-enquiry desk nearer the entrance may improve directions but leaves document-check capacity unchanged. The visible empty seat is therefore an unreliable guide to which alteration will reduce waiting.

Now change the example to a repair shop. Two mechanics have the same qualifications, but only one bay has the lift required for the waiting jobs. Cross-training would add little there; access to the lift limits the work. Returning to the idea of unusable spare capacity identifies a different resource to change.

For the seminar, draw the applicants or jobs, the required resources, and the resources actually available. Then place the proposed change on that drawing. The service-centre proposal changes permission to perform a task; the repair-shop proposal must change access to equipment. Comparing these cases shows why a queue model should represent what each server can do, rather than treating every person or desk as interchangeable.

# Following the divisibility argument

An even integer can be written as twice an integer. To show that the sum of two even integers is even, write the first as 2a and the second as 2b. Their sum is 2a + 2b, which factors as 2(a + b). Since a + b is an integer, the sum has the required form.

The letters stand for arbitrary integers. Choosing a = 3 and b = 5 gives a numerical illustration, but the proof works for any permitted choices. This is the difference between checking a particular sum and showing why every sum in the stated class has the property.

Students often pause at the final step because the factorization appears to settle everything. The definition requires twice an integer, however, so the status of the expression inside the brackets matters. The closure of integers under addition supplies that link. In a first proof course, saying it explicitly makes the dependence on the number system visible.

Before trying the next question, trace the completed argument in this order:

- Replace each even integer using the definition.
- Factor the common 2 out of the sum.
- Check that the expression left inside the brackets is an integer.
- Return to the definition of even.

Now attempt the same sequence for two odd integers, written as 2a + 1 and 2b + 1. The extra constants alter the bracket after factorization. Write that bracket out before deciding the parity of the result. Submit both the symbolic calculation and the sentence connecting its final form to the definition; together they show where the conclusion comes from.

A zero rainfall reading records an observed amount of none during the measurement interval. A blank reading records an absence of a usable measurement. The distinction matters because the same empty-looking entry can otherwise be interpreted in two incompatible ways.

In the field exercise, the observer reads the gauge at eight each morning and records rainfall for the preceding day. A dry gauge with a functioning collection system receives zero. If the observer cannot reach the site, the entry is marked missing even if the weather seemed dry elsewhere. The record describes the gauge observation, rather than a guess based on another location.

Suppose a week contains six recorded dry days and one missed visit. Replacing the blank with zero would report seven observed dry days. Keeping it missing preserves the fact that one day's amount is unknown. A weekly total calculated from the six observed days should therefore carry the number of days covered.

The distinction becomes especially important for averages. A spreadsheet can ignore blanks while including zeros. For a sequence with one recorded wet day, including six observed zeros produces a lower daily average than averaging only the wet reading. Both the values and the denominator need inspection before interpreting the result.

For submission, use separate fields for the amount and the observation status. The status field can distinguish a missed visit from a damaged gauge, while the amount field remains numerical whenever a valid amount was observed. Plot missing days as gaps rather than connecting them as dry observations. This makes the uncertainty visible at the point where readers would otherwise infer continuous measurement.

Using a room for an exhibition means giving up its best available alternative use during that period. The opportunity cost is the value of that forgone alternative, even when the museum already owns the room. Rent paid to an outside landlord and the cost of giving up an internal use are different items.

Suppose the museum is considering a six-week photographic exhibition. Its budget includes printing, insurance, and temporary partitions. Staff should check whether the insurance quotation covers installation and removal as well as the public opening dates. Otherwise the budget could leave part of the physical work outside the insured interval.

Attendance forecasts also need a clear unit. A count of entries to the room differs from a count of additional museum visitors. Someone who would have visited another gallery anyway can contribute to the first without increasing the second. A ticketing plan that records repeat entries will help separate those measures.

Ownership does not remove the opportunity cost: occupying the room with the exhibition still sacrifices the value of the best alternative use for those dates. A timetable of staff duties should accompany the cost sheet so installation hours are assigned to named teams. Particular attention is needed on the final Sunday, when the partitions must be removed before the next booking.

For the tutorial, prepare a list of information the museum must obtain before approving the exhibition. Separate confirmed quotations from estimates and identify who can supply each missing figure. The exercise ends with that information request; students are not expected to invent attendance or income for a programme whose competing room uses have yet to be costed.

Attendance forecasts also need a clear unit. A count of entries to the room differs from a count of additional museum visitors. Someone who would have visited another gallery anyway can contribute to the first without increasing the second. A ticketing plan that records repeat entries will help separate those measures.

Ownership does not remove the opportunity cost: occupying the room with the exhibition still sacrifices the value of the best alternative use for those dates. A timetable of staff duties should accompany the cost sheet so installation hours are assigned to named teams. Particular attention is needed on the final Sunday, when the partitions must be removed before the next booking.

For the tutorial, prepare a list of information the museum must obtain before approving the exhibition. Separate confirmed quotations from estimates and identify who can supply each missing figure. The exercise ends with that information request; students are not expected to invent attendance or income for a programme whose competing room uses have yet to be costed.

## Translating the joke in the doorway scene

A translation can preserve a word's reference while losing its sound pattern. A pun depending on similar sounds may then cease to work. In the doorway scene used for this exercise, the reply turns a visitor's family name into the name of a household object.

One option is to retain the name and explain the sound relationship in a footnote. The footnote makes the translator's intervention visible instead of presenting the explanation as part of the original dialogue. Another option is to invent a different verbal joke at the same point. That preserves the interruption's comic role but may change how the visitor is characterized.

Stage directions introduce a further constraint. The visitor is holding the object when the reply is spoken, so a replacement joke must still fit the action. Students should read the whole scene before choosing a substitute; a joke that works in an isolated line may make the next gesture difficult to understand.

The exercise sheet provides space for a literal version and a performance version. When similar sounds carry the joke, changing those sounds can remove the pun even if the translated words keep their ordinary reference. Under each version, record any change made to the visitor's name, the object, or the timing of the reply.

If you choose the footnote version, keep the note short enough to read without losing the speaker sequence. Putting this explanation below the text shows that it comes from the translator rather than from a speaker in the original scene. Bring both versions to the workshop, where another pair will read the dialogue aloud and identify any gesture that no longer matches the words.

# Interpreting shade measurements

A shaded patch can be cooler than a sunny patch at the same time, but the size of the difference depends on what is measured. Air temperature, the surface temperature of paving, and a person's radiant exposure are distinct quantities. The field class will measure the first two rather than treating a single thermometer reading as a complete account of comfort.

Place air sensors in matching ventilated shields at the same height. A sensor exposed directly to sunlight can warm above the surrounding air, confounding the quantity being measured with heating of the instrument. Record the placement with a photograph that shows the nearby wall and tree canopy.

For the paving measurement, use the same marked surface at each visit. Different paving materials can heat at different rates, so comparing a shaded stone slab with sunny asphalt would change two things together. The selected site has the same paving under both marked positions.

The afternoon comparison adds a new question. After the shadow moves, the formerly sunny slab may remain warmer because it stored heat earlier in the day. Shade at the moment of measurement therefore differs from shade throughout the preceding hours. Note when the shadow reaches each mark, then compare the cooling patterns rather than only the final temperatures.

The report should show the air and surface readings on separate axes with their measurement times. Use the morning comparison to discuss simultaneous shade and the afternoon sequence to discuss stored heat. If the surface difference persists while the air difference narrows, describe those two findings separately. That distinction tells the reader which part of the thermal environment changed and which remained similar.

# Scanning a signed form

Save the final scan as a single PDF, with the pages in the order shown on the form. Check that every signature and date is readable before sending it. The two routes below are alternatives depending on the equipment available.

## Using the office scanner

Remove staples and count the sheets before loading the feeder. Select PDF and choose double-sided scanning if any sheet has writing on the back. Preview the result on the computer, rotate sideways pages, and compare the page count with the original. Save the PDF in the case folder using the case number and signing date. Open the saved file to inspect the signatures and dates at normal reading size.

If the feeder takes two sheets together, remove the resulting scan and use the flatbed for those sheets. Align each one against the same corner mark. Keep a small paper slip beside the scanner to track the last completed page, especially when the form contains unnumbered attachments. Resume with the next sheet rather than relying on the application's displayed count, which may include the faulty scan.

## Using a phone

Place each page on a flat, contrasting surface in even light. Use the document-scanning mode rather than an ordinary photograph, keeping all four corners in view. Add each page to the same document and review the sequence before exporting. Check signatures and dates at normal reading size, then save one PDF in the case folder with the case number and signing date.

A raised fold can cast a shadow over handwriting. Flatten the sheet gently and move the light or phone until the shadow clears the text. Avoid correcting a shadow with an aggressive image filter that also removes faint pen strokes. Where the form includes an embossed mark, ask the case officer how it should be represented before treating a flat scan as complete.

## Final check

If a page is faint, improve the lighting or scanner settings and capture that page again. Compare the replacement with the paper before removing the first attempt from the document. Cropping can accidentally remove handwriting near an edge.

Attach the saved PDF to the case message and inspect the attachment name before sending. After transmission, retain the paper according to the case's records schedule. A successful upload confirms that a file reached the system; opening the attachment from the sent message confirms that the intended document was the one transmitted.

# Packing the costume cupboard

Give each storage box a number and put that number on its contents list. The number connects the list to the physical box even when several boxes look alike. Use the existing inventory sheet so the next production team can search by garment as well as by container.

Start with clean, dry costumes. Empty pockets, detach battery packs from illuminated accessories, and put loose buttons in a small labelled envelope. Items awaiting repair belong on the repair rail with a note describing the fault. Avoid packing a damp garment simply to finish the cupboard before the room booking ends.

Fold heavy garments at the bottom of a box and place lighter pieces above them. Wrap metal buckles so they cannot catch delicate fabric. Numbering the boxes links each inventory to the right container, so identical-looking boxes can still be distinguished. Record borrowed pieces separately and keep them near the door for return to their owners.

Photograph assembled outfits before separating their accessories. A single photograph of the hat, belt, shoes, and coat is easier to match during rehearsal than four unrelated close-ups. Add the photograph's file name to the inventory and copy the images into the production folder before clearing the camera.

Return full boxes to shelves within safe reach and leave the floor in front of the cupboard clear. Put the repair rail's list on the noticeboard so the wardrobe lead can assign those jobs at the next session. Keep the numbering system: matching the list number to the box number identifies which of the similar boxes holds the listed items. Lock the cupboard and return the key to the stage manager before leaving.

## Preparing the valley walk

Download the route map before leaving home. Parts of the valley have no mobile reception, so a map stored on the phone remains available where an online map may not load. This guide covers the marked riverside loop from the station to the old mill and back.

# Setting up the drinks table

Set the hot-water urn on the stable end table with its tap facing away from the main queue. Keep its cable behind the table and keep visitors away while the urn is being moved or filled. Use the venue's approved urn and follow its operating instructions; this checklist covers the table arrangement.

Place cups, tea bags, and sugar on the adjoining table. Leave a clear section directly in front of the tap so the person serving can set down a cup without reaching across food. Put cold drinks at the far end, where children can reach them without passing beneath the hot-water service.

Before opening, check that the drip tray is fitted and the table is dry. Keep a cloth for ordinary spills away from the food cloths. Agree which volunteer will serve hot water and which will restock cups. A separate helper can take cash or tokens if the event uses them, keeping the serving area from becoming a payment queue.

When the urn needs attention, pause service and clear visitors from that end of the table before following the venue's refill procedure. The queue may have moved closer during the event, so restore the gap rather than assuming the opening arrangement still holds. Leave any lifting to staff authorized by the venue.

At closing, switch off the urn as directed and leave it in place until venue staff say it is ready to empty or move. Collect unused supplies from the adjoining table first. Dry the floor, count the cups being returned, and tell the caretaker about any leak or damaged cable before the equipment goes back into storage.

# Recording the windowsill trial

Write the variety and sowing date on a label in each tray. Seedlings can look alike before their true leaves develop, so the label preserves an identification you may be unable to recover by sight. Record germination against the sowing date rather than the day you first notice growth. That gives each batch the same starting point when comparing how long emergence took.

Use clean trays with drainage holes and place them inside a watertight outer tray to protect the sill. Fill each cell with the same compost and sow according to the packet's depth guidance. Keep the packets together so you can check the supplier's instructions later.

Choose a position with suitable light for the varieties you are growing. Rotate the outer tray if one side receives much stronger light, and note the rotation in the record. The tray label keeps the variety identifiable while young plants are still too similar to tell apart. Check moisture with a fingertip rather than adding water simply because the surface has changed colour.

Look beneath the trays at the weekly check. Water collecting there may come from a recent watering or from a small leak in the inner tray. Empty the outer tray and dry the sill, then inspect the cell tray before putting it back. If a tray is cracked, move it onto a sound support before carrying it so the cells do not separate in your hands. Keep any dropped seedling apart until you can see whether its stem is damaged.

Use a notebook page for each variety, with columns for sowing, first emergence, and the number of occupied cells. Counting from sowing gives every batch a common starting event, unlike counting from when you happen to notice the shoots. Photograph the trays from the same position when making the weekly entry.

When roots fill the cells, follow the growing instructions for moving the plants into larger pots. Handle them carefully and prepare the new pots before starting. Leave space in the notebook for the transfer date and any losses during the following week. Store the notebook with the unused packets when the trial finishes.

## Sending photographs to the local archive

Choose the highest-resolution original available rather than a copy saved from a messaging thread. Put the files in a folder named with your surname and the donation date. Keep your own copy while the archive checks the transfer.

Create a plain text note identifying each photograph by file name. Add the place, approximate date, and names you know. Use 'unknown' for a person you cannot identify, and distinguish an approximate decade from an exact date written on the back. If a caption came from someone else, name that person as the source.

The archive also needs to know who took each photograph, if known, and who is offering the copy. A family member holding a print may have different information from the photographer. Include an email address where staff can ask about permissions and the proposed public description.

Send the folder using the transfer link in the archive's reply. If the connection fails, keep the folder intact and contact the archive with the transfer name rather than repeatedly sending separate attachments. Staff can check what arrived and issue a replacement link if needed.

Before you send, use this check:

- The folder contains the highest-resolution originals you have.
- The note matches captions to file names and marks uncertain dates or names.
- The note identifies the photographer where known and gives your contact address.
- You have retained your own copy.

After transfer, staff will confirm receipt and discuss the catalogue description. Wait for that message before disposing of any temporary working copies. Keep the original prints and their envelopes together until the archive has finished checking dates and inscriptions.

# Cleaning the watercolour brushes

Rinse each brush in clean water as soon as you finish painting. Work colour out gently with your fingers, following the brush maker's cleaning instructions. Let the brush dry with its bristles pointing down or lying flat. Water left running into the handle can loosen the attachment between the bristles and the handle.

Use two rinse jars during the session, one for the first wash and one for the cleaner final rinse. Change both when their water becomes heavily coloured. Wipe excess paint from the mixing palette before washing it so the sink is easier to clean afterwards. Keep cleaning supplies separate from cups used for drinking.

After rinsing a brush, reshape the tip while the bristles are damp. Lay it on a clean cloth where the tip will not be pressed against another object. Drying with the bristles downward keeps water from travelling into the handle and weakening the bristle attachment. Avoid putting a protective cap onto a brush that has not yet dried.

Once everything is dry, return the brushes to their tray, grouping them by size so the next class can find the required set. Check the handles for names and place any borrowed brush in the return envelope. Record damaged tips on the supply sheet rather than quietly putting them back with the usable set.

Clean the jars, wipe the table, and leave the drying cloth spread out in the designated place. The reason for keeping the wet bristles below the handle is to prevent water reaching the joint that holds them in place. Put the completed supply sheet in the tutor's folder before locking the cupboard.

paragraphs.text: Rinse each brush in clean water as soon as you finish painting. Work colour out gently with your fingers, following the brush maker's cleaning instructions. Let the brush dry with its bristles pointing down or lying flat. Water left running into the handle can loosen the attachment between the bristles and the handle.

Use two rinse jars during the session, one for the first wash and one for the cleaner final rinse. Change both when their water becomes heavily coloured. Wipe excess paint from the mixing palette before washing it so the sink is easier to clean afterwards. Keep cleaning supplies separate from cups used for drinking.

After rinsing a brush, reshape the tip while the bristles are damp. Lay it on a clean cloth where the tip will not be pressed against another object. Drying with the bristles downward keeps water from travelling into the handle and weakening the bristle attachment. Avoid putting a protective cap onto a brush that has not yet dried.

Once everything is dry, return the brushes to their tray, grouping them by size so the next class can find the required set. Check the handles for names and place any borrowed brush in the return envelope. Record damaged tips on the supply sheet rather than quietly putting them back with the usable set.

Clean the jars, wipe the table, and leave the drying cloth spread out in the designated place. The reason for keeping the wet bristles below the handle is to prevent water reaching the joint that holds them in place. Put the completed supply sheet in the tutor's folder before locking the cupboard.

# Editing the oral-history session

Copy the recorder's files into the project folder before opening the editing application. Keep the original audio files. Work on duplicates so cuts and noise adjustments can be compared with the unedited session if a transcript query arises later.

## Naming the working copy

Use the interview code and recording date in the file name. Add a version number when saving an editing project, and keep associated media in the folder created by the application. Moving a linked audio file after saving can leave the project unable to find its source. Open the project once after copying it to the shared drive to check those links.

## Making the edit

Start with long interruptions that the participant has agreed may be removed. Leave room around speech when cutting so breaths and final consonants remain audible. Listen across each join at normal speed. Retain the original recordings. For a section with background noise, compare a short processed sample with the untreated copy before applying the setting to the whole session.

## Export and handover

Export the agreed listening copy in the format requested by the archive. Play its beginning, one edited join, and its ending before uploading. Record the export date and the working-project version on the handover sheet. If the application offers several audio channels, check that the export contains the intended speakers rather than only the microphone nearest the interviewer.

Send the listening copy and handover sheet through the archive's transfer route. The archivist will confirm receipt and any access restrictions before the session is catalogued. Leave the editing project in the committee folder until that confirmation arrives and the transcript has been checked against the exported file.

## Repotting the office spider plant

Choose a pot only a little wider than the root ball and use a suitable houseplant compost. Clear the drainage holes before adding compost. Blocked holes prevent excess water from escaping and can leave the roots sitting in saturated compost. Put a tray beneath the pot to protect the windowsill.

Water the plant lightly beforehand if the root ball is very dry. Spread paper on the table, support the base of the leaves, and ease the plant out without pulling on individual leaves. If the old pot grips the roots, work around its edge rather than forcing the stem. Check the root ball and remove loose old compost gently.

Set a shallow layer of new compost in the pot, place the plant at its previous depth, and fill the space around it. Firm lightly with your fingers. Leave room below the rim for watering, and keep compost out of the centre of the leaf cluster. Turn the pot as you work to check that the plant remains upright.

After watering, let the pot finish draining before returning it to the sill. If the openings are obstructed, surplus water stays in the pot and the roots remain in waterlogged compost. Empty the tray once runoff has collected, and check the sill for spills. The first watering may settle the compost enough to expose a small gap around the edge; top up that gap without burying the plant more deeply.

Write the repotting date on the office plant sheet. Resume watering according to the compost's condition, and leave the plant out of strong direct afternoon sun while it settles into the new pot.

# Preparing the lecture recording

Use the wired connection for the presentation laptop. The wireless signal is weak at the lectern, while the tested cable gives the laptop a stable connection there. The recording computer is already connected separately and should remain on its existing port.

Open the slides from the local project folder before the speaker arrives. Check the first slide, a slide containing video, and the final slide on the room display. If the speaker has brought a revised file, save it with the delivery time in the name so staff can distinguish it from the rehearsal copy.

Check the captions on embedded videos. A caption file stored beside a video may work on the speaker's computer but fail after only the slides are copied. Run the clip from the actual lectern computer and watch the captioned section on the room display. Ask the speaker for any missing media before the audience enters. For a clip that needs a spoken introduction, mark the point where the chair should pause rather than allowing automatic playback to cut across the introduction.

Ask the speaker to read two sentences while you monitor the recording input. Check that the room microphone and the recording track both receive the intended voice. The wired option is preferable at the lectern because its tested connection avoids the weak wireless signal. Put fresh batteries in the handheld question microphone and leave its spare set with the technician.

Confirm the speaker's permission to record and note any portion that should be excluded from the published version. The chair should announce the recording before the first question from the audience. Keep a note of the time if someone requests that a contribution be removed, rather than relying on an approximate memory after the session.

At the end, stop the recording and confirm that the session file has saved before shutting down either computer. Copy the chair's exclusion notes into the recording folder and send the editor the file location. For this presentation, the cable remains the better connection. Coil the lectern lead loosely and return the question microphone to its charging position once the audience has left.

## Sorting the donated photograph box

Handle prints by their edges with clean, dry hands as directed by the archive. Touching the image surface can leave oils and marks that become part of the stored print. If a print is damaged, stuck to another print, or showing possible mould, stop and ask the archivist before separating or cleaning it.

Keep the donor's envelopes and the order in which they were received. Put a temporary number on a separate slip rather than writing on a photograph. Copy any caption into the intake sheet, preserving uncertain spellings until the donor or another source can clarify them. A question mark in an old caption should remain visible in the transcription.

Place each loose print in the enclosure supplied for it. Use the intake number to connect the enclosure with the spreadsheet row. Finger contact with the picture can deposit oils and leave lasting marks, which is why the print should be held at its edges. Record dimensions in the agreed unit and keep landscape and portrait measurements in the same column order.

For groups that clearly arrived together, record the group relationship before giving individual items their numbers. A holiday envelope may help date several otherwise uncaptioned views. Photograph the envelope front and back and link those images to the group record. Return letters or receipts to their original position once they have been described.

At the end of the session, count the enclosed prints against the intake sheet and record any unresolved identification questions. Put the whole group in the assigned archive box, leaving the donor correspondence in its separate folder. Tell the archivist which items need attention before the next volunteer shift begins.

paragraphs.text: Handle prints by their edges with clean, dry hands as directed by the archive. Touching the image surface can leave oils and marks that become part of the stored print. If a print is damaged, stuck to another print, or showing possible mould, stop and ask the archivist before separating or cleaning it.

Keep the donor's envelopes and the order in which they were received. Put a temporary number on a separate slip rather than writing on a photograph. Copy any caption into the intake sheet, preserving uncertain spellings until the donor or another source can clarify them. A question mark in an old caption should remain visible in the transcription.

Place each loose print in the enclosure supplied for it. Use the intake number to connect the enclosure with the spreadsheet row. Finger contact with the picture can deposit oils and leave lasting marks, which is why the print should be held at its edges. Record dimensions in the agreed unit and keep landscape and portrait measurements in the same column order.

For groups that clearly arrived together, record the group relationship before giving individual items their numbers. A holiday envelope may help date several otherwise uncaptioned views. Photograph the envelope front and back and link those images to the group record. Return letters or receipts to their original position once they have been described.

At the end of the session, count the enclosed prints against the intake sheet and record any unresolved identification questions. Put the whole group in the assigned archive box, leaving the donor correspondence in its separate folder. Tell the archivist which items need attention before the next volunteer shift begins.

documents.text:
# Cleaning the laminated display boards

Check the board supplier's care sheet and choose a cleaner approved for the surface. Try the cleaner on a hidden patch first and let that patch dry. A product can alter the finish even when it removes the dirt, and the dry test shows whether the appearance has changed.

Remove the paper inserts and label them with the board number before starting. Put screws and clips in a tray so they cannot fall into the waste paper. If a board has an electrical lighting strip attached, follow the venue's isolation procedure before cleaning around it and leave any damaged connection for the technician.

Use a soft cloth with the amount of cleaner specified on the care sheet. Work on one small area at a time and avoid flooding joints or exposed edges. Turn the cloth frequently so collected dirt is lifted away rather than spread across the next section. Stubborn adhesive needs the supplier's recommended method; scraping with a metal blade can damage the face.

Wipe away residue as directed and allow the board to dry fully before replacing the inserts. Inspect it from an angle under the room lighting, where streaks and missed patches are easier to see. Refit the clips without overtightening and check that the insert sits flat inside its frame.

Record any lifted edge or cracked corner on the display-maintenance sheet and keep that board aside for inspection. The hidden test matters because removing dirt and preserving the finish are separate results: the dried patch reveals any change caused by the cleaner. Return the cleaned boards to their numbered slots and store the cleaning materials in the locked cupboard.

documents.text:
We opened the bicycle repair morning in the school courtyard, with two workstands beneath the covered walkway. We gave each bicycle a numbered tag so the mechanics could take repairs in arrival order without asking everyone when they had joined the queue. The tags were left over from the previous summer's equipment sale.

The first hour was mostly punctures. I checked names and telephone numbers while Leila counted the spare tubes. One visitor brought a folding bicycle with a tyre size we did not stock, so we wrote down the size and the name of a nearby shop. He stayed to watch while his daughter helped pump up another bicycle.

By eleven, the wind had started lifting the paper forms from the table. I borrowed a clipboard from the office and moved the box of completed sheets beneath a chair. The tags let the mechanics follow arrival order without repeatedly asking people who had come first. A volunteer brought tea in a flask and balanced the cups on an unopened carton of cleaning rags.

We stopped accepting new jobs at half past twelve. The last repair involved replacing a brake cable, and the owner waited while the mechanic checked its operation in the empty part of the yard. Leila counted the remaining tubes and put the unused cable ends into their divided box.

Numbering the bicycles had been intended to preserve the arrival sequence without relying on the owners to reconstruct it. I took the cash tin to the office, where the caretaker counted the donations with me. We left the workstands folded beside the stage door for collection on Monday and swept the small pieces of wire into the workshop waste container.

# The missing drawer label

When I arrived at the archive, the shallow drawer nearest the window had a blank label holder. Our map request slip said only 'river survey, lower drawer', so I began with the cabinet on that side of the room. There were four lower drawers, each deep enough to hold several folders.

Marta brought the old cabinet plan from the office. Its pencil numbers matched marks inside the drawer handles, and we found the survey beneath a set of road plans. I carried the folder to the reading table while she checked the other drawers against the plan. Two had exchanged contents during last month's cleaning.

The researcher spent the morning comparing the survey with a later street map. At lunch she asked for tracing paper and a longer ruler. I found both in the education cupboard, where the ruler was still attached to a demonstration board with a strip of tape.

During the afternoon, Marta printed new drawer labels and updated the cabinet plan. She put the survey's full reference on its folder and copied that reference onto the request slip. The researcher used it in her notes before returning the maps to the desk.

The next morning a second reader asked for the same river survey. I took his slip to the window cabinet and went straight to the newly labelled drawer. Inside, the matching folder reference was visible without lifting the road plans. I brought it out before Marta had finished entering his name in the day book. She filed the old pencil plan with the cleaning record and put the revised copy by the request forms.

documents.text:
At the rehearsal, the director wrote 'Leave room for the door' across the top of the stage plan. The set included a long dining table, and its first position stopped the kitchen door opening fully. We moved the table towards the audience and marked its feet with tape.

The cast arrived at seven carrying scripts and takeaway cups. During the first scene, a tray of wooden fruit rolled off a chair and scattered beneath the table. We stopped while the youngest actor retrieved the apples, then added a folded cloth under the tray for the next run.

The lighting operator had been watching from the back row. She asked us to pause at the point where the visitor removed his hat, since his face fell into shadow when he turned towards the table. We held the positions while she adjusted a lamp, then ran the entrance again. The change caught the visitor but left the actor beside the window too bright. She wrote both positions on her sheet and said she would finish the adjustment during the break. I put a small mark near the visitor's chair for the next run.

At the interval, Jo brought in the costume rail. It was too wide to turn through the side entrance with its extension arm raised. She lowered the arm, moved the rail into the dressing room, and hung the coats in scene order. I copied the new table marks onto the plan while the director discussed the final entrance with the cast.

A missing waistcoat delayed the restart. Its owner found it in the prop cupboard, folded inside the box containing the dinner napkins. Jo checked the pockets for the letter needed in the second scene and returned the empty envelope to the writing desk. The actor tried the waistcoat with his coat on top and found he could reach the pocket without opening the coat. We added that movement to the run rather than leaving it for the dress rehearsal.

We ran the last scene twice. This time the kitchen door cleared the table, but the actor carrying the covered dish had nowhere to put it down. Jo removed the fruit tray and moved a small stand beside the chair. The dish landed there cleanly on the second attempt.

As we packed away, I wheeled the costume rail back towards the side entrance with its arm still extended. 'Leave room for the door,' Jo said, tapping the top of my stage plan. I lowered the arm and turned the rail through. She put the plan in the prompt folder, with the new stand marked beside the table.

A missing waistcoat delayed the restart. Its owner found it in the prop cupboard, folded inside the box containing the dinner napkins. Jo checked the pockets for the letter needed in the second scene and returned the empty envelope to the writing desk. The actor tried the waistcoat with his coat on top and found he could reach the pocket without opening the coat. We added that movement to the run rather than leaving it for the dress rehearsal.

We ran the last scene twice. This time the kitchen door cleared the table, but the actor carrying the covered dish had nowhere to put it down. Jo removed the fruit tray and moved a small stand beside the chair. The dish landed there cleanly on the second attempt.

As we packed away, I wheeled the costume rail back towards the side entrance with its arm still extended. 'Leave room for the door,' Jo said, tapping the top of my stage plan. I lowered the arm and turned the rail through. She put the plan in the prompt folder, with the new stand marked beside the table.

# Saturday at the covered market

We moved the sign-in table inside because rain had soaked the forms at the previous market. The yellow badges identified stallholders, allowing the gate volunteer to distinguish them from early shoppers. At seven thirty, there were already three vans waiting beside the loading door.

The baker had brought an extra folding table, which fitted into the gap left by a cancelled flower stall. We checked that it did not narrow the route to the toilets and added its position to the plan. Two volunteers carried the empty bread crates to the loading area while he arranged the loaves.

A jewellery seller arrived without the small mirror she normally used on her stall. The caretaker found a spare in the dressing room and helped her prop it against a wooden display block. They checked the angle from the customer's side before putting out the trays. Next to her, the book dealer discovered that his price signs still showed the previous venue's currency symbol. He covered the symbols with small stickers while his assistant stacked the books. I fetched a fresh roll of stickers from the office so they could finish before the doors opened.

At registration, I found that the printed list used last month's table numbers. Bringing registration under the roof kept the paperwork out of the rain that had damaged it last time. I crossed out the old numbers, copied the new ones from the plan, and asked each trader to check the position before unloading.

The coffee machine took longer to heat than expected. The cafe opened with tea and cold drinks while the technician checked its water supply. Outside, a bus had stopped across the entrance, and the first shoppers came in through the side gate instead. The yellow badges showed which arrivals had stalls, making them distinguishable from customers arriving before opening.

The children's craft table opened at half past nine. Its organizer had brought newspaper for the floor and small aprons borrowed from the school. She asked for another waste bin, and we moved the empty one from the office into the space behind her chairs. A parent helped shorten the apron ties before the first group began painting. When one paint pot leaked, they lifted the newspaper together and replaced the affected sheets without moving the whole table. I brought a mop for the small patch beyond the paper.

By ten, the main entrance was clear and the cafe was serving coffee. I collected the corrected lists from the registration table and took a copy to the gate. When the last van had unloaded, we folded the spare trolley and put it behind the office door, leaving the loading route free for collections at the end of the day.

The shop had installed a return tray beside the till to keep customer returns apart from books waiting to be sold. Staff had twice shelved a returned book before its refund was recorded. I came in on Tuesday to help with the annual stock count, just as the carpenter was removing the tray's packaging.

We began upstairs with the travel shelves. Someone had placed a walking guide among the language books, and several maps had slipped behind the bottom row. I counted while Omar entered the figures on a tablet. Every half hour we saved the sheet and moved the small counting marker to the next shelf.

At lunch, the delivery driver brought three cartons of diaries. Their covers looked similar, but one carton contained the larger format, which had a separate stock code. Omar checked the invoice while I put a sample of each size on the desk for the afternoon team. The cardboard went into the recycling cage behind the shop.

We finished the children's section shortly after four. Two illustrated books had damaged jackets, so the manager set them aside to price separately. The tray separated returned books from sale stock so staff would not put them on a shelf before entering the refund. Beside it, she arranged the new diary samples on a stand with their prices facing the queue.

Before leaving, I checked the upstairs shelves for counting slips and returned the tablet to its charger. Omar printed the discrepancy list for the manager, who planned to compare it with the previous week's deliveries. We locked the side door and carried the flattened diary cartons to the cage on our way out.

# Clearing the school hall

Before the jumble sale opened, the caretaker asked us to keep the fire exit clear. We moved a rack of coats away from it and taped a stall boundary on the floor. The rack then fitted beside the stage steps, where a volunteer could watch the bags left beneath it.

The first customers arrived with coins and shopping bags. I worked on the book stall, sorting a donation that had come in after the prices were printed. One box held school atlases with different editions, so we grouped them by publication date rather than assuming their matching covers meant identical contents.

At noon, a visitor asked whether we could hold a small table while she collected her car. The furniture team wrote her name on a card and put the table in the collection bay. She returned twenty minutes later, and two volunteers carried it out through the main entrance.

When the sale ended, we brought trolleys from the store to move the remaining boxes. A pile of empty cartons began growing beside the fire exit as people cleared their stalls. The caretaker asked us to clear that exit again before the trolleys started moving. We took the cartons straight to the recycling area, then loaded the books from the marked stall boundary.

The hall was empty by three. We lifted the tape from the floor, counted the borrowed trestles, and checked behind the stage curtains for bags. The coat rack went back into the store with its wheels locked. I handed the collection cards to the organizer so she could contact the owners of the two items still waiting in the bay.
