We moved the rehearsal to the upstairs room because roadworks outside the ground-floor windows made the piano difficult to hear. The room had been used for language classes, and its tables were still arranged in small groups. I arrived early with Daniel to stack them against the back wall.

The choir's folders had been delivered to the usual room, so Daniel went downstairs to collect them while I set out chairs. We found thirty chairs and borrowed another six from the meeting room. A narrow gap remained beside the radiator for the keyboard case.

At seven, the singers began arriving, some carrying the revised score sent that afternoon. We printed eight additional copies on the office printer. The upstairs location avoided the road noise that had been drowning out the piano downstairs. I put the spare copies on a chair by the entrance and wrote the new page number on the board.

The first run stopped twice at the same change of tempo. Our accompanist marked the cue in his score, and the conductor asked the altos to sing the passage without the other parts. By the break, the ending was together, although several people still wanted the note names on the rehearsal recording.

Holding the session above ground level kept us away from the roadworks that obscured the piano in the lower room. After rehearsal, Daniel recorded the difficult passage on his phone while the accompanist played it slowly. We restored the tables to their classroom groups, counted the borrowed chairs, and took the folders down to the office. The conductor sent the recording to the choir before the last bus left the square.

## The allotment store on Sunday

We spent Sunday morning emptying the allotment store so the roof contractor could inspect the leak. Before moving anything, Priya photographed each shelf and wrote the shelf numbers on the boxes we would use. The committee wanted the equipment returned to the same places afterwards.

The long tools went under the covered washing area. We tied them in small bundles and left the paths clear. The seed tins stayed dry in the greenhouse, while the paper records went into Priya's car. One watering can had split along its base, so we marked it for replacement rather than putting it with the usable equipment.

The contractor arrived at eleven and checked the roof from the platform he had brought. He found a loose edge above the rear shelf and arranged to return on Wednesday with the required materials. We covered the tool bundles and wrote their location on the noticeboard. Priya emailed the plot holders about the temporary arrangements. The greenhouse key remained in the usual key box, and anyone needing the paper records could contact her. I took the split watering can to the committee shed so its replacement would be discussed at the next meeting.

Before leaving, we checked the temporary arrangement against our list: tools under the washing-area cover, seeds in the greenhouse, records with Priya, and the damaged can in the committee shed. The photographs and numbered boxes were ready for putting everything back after Wednesday's repair. We locked the empty store and left the door space clear for the contractor.

# Choosing the exhibition tables

At the start of the planning morning, I suggested using the hall's narrow tables for the pottery display. They would leave a wider route between the exhibits. Ruth had brought the plan from last year's show, which used larger tables borrowed from the school.

We laid out both sizes with masking tape before moving any furniture. The larger tables gave us room for deep display boards, but their corners left little space where the route turned towards the refreshment hatch. We pushed a loaded trolley through that turn and had to move one taped corner to get it past.

The narrow-table layout handled the turn easily. Its problem was the tall centrepiece, whose base would overhang the table. Ruth measured the base and found that it fitted the low plinth stored behind the stage. Putting it there also brought the top within the planned lighting area.

After lunch, we tried the boards on the narrow tables using the actual cloths and supports. The shallower arrangement held the smaller work securely, and the large bowls fitted on the end table with space between them. We marked those positions on the plan and photographed the trolley passing the hatch.

We chose the narrow tables, with the centrepiece on the separate plinth. That kept the wider route I had wanted while the board test and plinth solved the display-space problems we had found. Ruth cancelled the school collection and sent the revised plan to the exhibitors. I left the tape down until the hall manager had checked it, then rolled up the unused large-table cloths and put them back in the store.

# Moving the walking-group notices

## The board

We decided to keep the existing noticeboard because its glass cover protected the walking-group notices from rain. The frame needed a new fixing, and the caretaker had ordered one. We used the morning meeting to sort the papers that would go back inside it.

## The papers

Several route sheets were out of date. Helen checked the walks against the current programme while I removed faded telephone numbers from the bottom strip. We kept the large map, which still showed the meeting point clearly, and printed a fresh copy of the bus timetable. The printer ran out of black ink halfway through, so Helen collected a cartridge from the office.

## Fitting

The caretaker arrived after lunch with the new bracket. He asked us to clear the bench beneath the board while he worked, and we carried the plant pots into the entrance. Keeping the covered noticeboard was the right choice for protecting the notices from rain. Once the frame was secured, he checked the lock and left the spare key with reception.

## Finishing

We arranged the sheets in date order and put the next walk nearest the opening edge. Helen added a small envelope for printed route copies, then counted how many would fit without hiding the map. The old sheets went into the paper bin except for one programme retained in the group's annual folder.

At four, the leader of Saturday's walk came to collect her copies. She corrected the meeting time on one draft before we printed the final set. I returned the plant pots to the bench, and Helen put the noticeboard key on the labelled hook behind reception.

The library's delivery van arrived an hour late on Thursday because a road closure had diverted it through the next town. We moved the reserved-book collections to the afternoon and put a note on the front desk. I telephoned the two readers who had said they could come only before lunch.

While we waited, Amira cleared space in the returns room. The history society had brought back six crates after its exhibition, and the crates occupied the place where the van's boxes usually went. We checked their contents against the loan sheet and moved the emptied crates beneath the workbench.

The driver arrived with eleven boxes and an extra envelope containing a replacement map. One box had a torn corner, so we counted its contents before signing. Everything was present. Amira took the map to the reading room, where a researcher had been waiting to compare it with a volume already on her desk.

The delay affected the outreach run differently. The volunteer who carried books to the residential home left at noon, before we had sorted the van's boxes. Her delivery contained the books already on the outreach shelf, but the new large-print titles would have to wait until Monday. I added them to the next-run list and called the activities coordinator.

By three, most reserved books were ready for collection. One of the morning readers came after receiving my call; the other asked us to hold her books until Saturday. Amira filed the signed delivery sheet and put the large-print titles in a separate crate marked for Monday. The late van had shifted collections within the day and outreach across the weekend, so the two follow-up lists stayed separate.

The museum gave each borrowed object a temporary number so photographs and condition notes could be matched to the right item before formal accessioning. On Monday, I helped record a box of household tools brought in by a family from the village. The donor stayed for the first hour to explain which relative had used them.

We started with the largest items because they needed most of the padded table. The wooden handle on a flour scoop had a split near its end. I photographed the split beside a scale, and Eva entered the donor's account in the intake form. She kept the family story in a separate field from the description of the object.

The smallest items came in an old biscuit tin. There were buttons, a measuring tape, and two paper packets containing needles. Eva photographed the packets without opening them and asked the collections manager to inspect their condition. We put the tin on a separate tray while she worked.

At the end of the afternoon, I copied the photographs to the intake folder and checked their focus on the office monitor. Temporary numbers connected the photographs and condition descriptions with their corresponding objects while the formal accession records were still pending. Two images needed retaking because the polished metal reflected the ceiling lights.

We left those objects on the padded table with the camera settings written on a card. Eva sent the donor a receipt listing the material received and the questions still to be answered. Before closing, the collections manager covered the trays and asked us to leave the tin untouched until she could examine the paper packets in better light.

paragraphs.text: The museum gave each borrowed object a temporary number so photographs and condition notes could be matched to the right item before formal accessioning. On Monday, I helped record a box of household tools brought in by a family from the village. The donor stayed for the first hour to explain which relative had used them.

We started with the largest items because they needed most of the padded table. The wooden handle on a flour scoop had a split near its end. I photographed the split beside a scale, and Eva entered the donor's account in the intake form. She kept the family story in a separate field from the description of the object.

The smallest items came in an old biscuit tin. There were buttons, a measuring tape, and two paper packets containing needles. Eva photographed the packets without opening them and asked the collections manager to inspect their condition. We put the tin on a separate tray while she worked.

At the end of the afternoon, I copied the photographs to the intake folder and checked their focus on the office monitor. Temporary numbers connected the photographs and condition descriptions with their corresponding objects while the formal accession records were still pending. Two images needed retaking because the polished metal reflected the ceiling lights.

We left those objects on the padded table with the camera settings written on a card. Eva sent the donor a receipt listing the material received and the questions still to be answered. Before closing, the collections manager covered the trays and asked us to leave the tin untouched until she could examine the paper packets in better light.

We put the children's coats on low hooks so they could collect them without an adult lifting each one down. The trays under the boots were there to catch mud before it spread onto the classroom floor. It was the first wet morning after the new entrance cupboards had been fitted.

At nine, the class went out to inspect the garden beds. They found a row of beans that had come loose from its supports, and the teacher brought string from the shed. I stayed near the gate with the attendance sheet while two children fetched the watering cans. The rain stopped before they had filled them.

Back inside, the teacher laid leaves and seed pods on the science table. Having the hooks within reach meant the children could take their own coats rather than waiting for an adult to retrieve them. I helped find magnifying glasses and put a sheet of white paper beneath the smallest seeds so they were easier to see.

After lunch, we prepared the display labels. Some children dictated their observations, while others drew the bean stems with their new ties. The boot trays collected the mud so it would not be carried across the classroom floor. A parent volunteer mounted the drawings on dark card and added the date at the bottom.

Before home time, the teacher photographed the finished display for the class journal. I rinsed the watering cans and returned the string to the shed. We put the seed pods in a lidded observation box and left the drawings on the drying rack. The last child to leave carried a spare jumper in a paper bag because his own had been left on the garden bench.

## Checking the hall before the concert

The morning team planned to leave the ticket table beside the main entrance and the programmes on the shelf behind it. The evening volunteers would arrive after the sound check, so we wrote those positions on their handover sheet.

While setting up, we found that the card reader would connect only near the office door. Its usual cable had a damaged connector, and the replacement lead was shorter. The hall manager moved the payment table to the office side and tested it with a small transaction, which she then refunded. We erased the old ticket-table position from the plan.

The programme shelf could remain where it was. We divided the programmes into two piles, keeping a small number behind the payment table for people who paid by card and sending the larger pile to the entrance volunteer. The volunteer checking advance tickets would also direct people towards their seats.

After the sound check, a speaker stand was still occupying the corner beside the office. The technician moved it to the stage before the doors opened. I checked the cable route with the hall manager and taped down the approved crossing point using the venue's cable cover.

At five thirty, the evening team arrived. I showed them the payment table by the office, the programmes at both stations, and the advance-ticket position at the entrance. We went through those locations on the corrected handover sheet while they stood at their stations. The entrance volunteer asked for another pen, and the payment volunteer completed a reader check. I left the corrected plan beside the cash tin and took the superseded copy to the office recycling tray.

The first box was empty. There was nothing inside it except a folded packing sheet. We had opened it expecting the replacement reading lamps, and for a moment all three of us looked beneath the loose paper as though the lamps might be hidden there.

The supplier's delivery note listed two boxes. The driver checked his van and found the second behind a stack of flat cartons. It contained the lamps, each wrapped separately with its base screws in a taped bag. We signed for the delivery and carried everything into the reading room before opening the wrapping.

One lamp needed its base tightened. Another had its switch in a different position from the sample pictured on the order. Mina checked the model number and found that it matched the revised catalogue entry. We set both lamps on the table near the socket and asked the caretaker to complete the electrical checks required by the library.

While he worked, I flattened the packaging. The box we had first opened turned out to have held the display stands sent on approval the previous month. Someone had put it back in the delivery area with its old label attached. Mina crossed out that label and wrote the stand-return reference on a fresh one.

By closing time, the checked lamps were beside the reading chairs. I came back for the supposedly empty box and found the two rejected stands packed inside it, with Mina's return sheet on top. This time I checked the new label before lifting it. The caretaker opened the loading door, and we left the parcel in the marked collection space for the next morning's van.

# A morning at the riverside cafe

We agreed to keep the paper order pad because the cafe's tablet lost its connection on the terrace, leaving staff unable to send those orders to the kitchen. The manager had already reported the fault and was waiting for an engineer's visit. I covered the terrace shift on Friday while the regular server attended a training session.

Before opening, we carried the chairs out in pairs and checked the tables for wobbling feet. One needed a small replacement pad, which the caretaker fetched from his toolbox. The weather was clear, but we left the umbrellas tied until the wind dropped. The breakfast menus went into their weighted holders.

The first group arrived after a rowing practice. They pushed two tables together and ordered toast, porridge, and coffee. I checked the milk options with the kitchen because the printed menu had not yet been updated. The cook wrote the available choices on a card, which we put beside the till.

At eleven, the manager brought the delivery invoices for signing. Keeping the paper pad was the sensible choice while the terrace connection prevented the tablet from passing orders to the kitchen. I checked the number of juice cartons against the invoice and moved the empty crates away from the cellar door. A second supplier had substituted smaller jars of jam, so the manager recorded the changed quantity before approving that bill.

The lunch server arrived at noon. We counted the clean cutlery, wiped the menu holders, and exchanged the wobbling table for one from the store. I left the signed invoices in the office tray and took the empty crates to the collection point behind the kitchen.

The first group arrived after a rowing practice. They pushed two tables together and ordered toast, porridge, and coffee. I checked the milk options with the kitchen because the printed menu had not yet been updated. The cook wrote the available choices on a card, which we put beside the till.

At eleven, the manager brought the delivery invoices for signing. Keeping the paper pad was the sensible choice while the terrace connection prevented the tablet from passing orders to the kitchen. I checked the number of juice cartons against the invoice and moved the empty crates away from the cellar door. A second supplier had substituted smaller jars of jam, so the manager recorded the changed quantity before approving that bill.

The lunch server arrived at noon. We counted the clean cutlery, wiped the menu holders, and exchanged the wobbling table for one from the store. I left the signed invoices in the office tray and took the empty crates to the collection point behind the kitchen.

# Making a community recipe booklet

Ask contributors to state how many portions each recipe makes. A serving count allows someone cooking for a different number of people to adjust the ingredient quantities. Keep the contributor's stated yield even when you change the layout or shorten the introduction.

Set up one page style before entering the recipes. Put the ingredient list beside the method if there is room, and keep the units consistent within each recipe. Where a contributor uses a cup or spoon as a measure, ask which size they mean before replacing it with another unit.

Read each method against its ingredient list. Check for ingredients that appear in the instructions but are missing from the list, and for ingredients listed without any instruction about when to add them. Ask the contributor to settle those questions rather than guessing from another recipe with a similar name.

A recipe's serving count tells the reader how many people the stated quantities will feed. That lets a household increase or reduce the ingredients to suit its own table. Preserve that number when preparing the pages; changing the page design or cutting introductory wording should leave the contributor's yield intact.

Choose photographs after the text has been checked. A photo should show the dish the recipe describes, and the contributor should approve any picture taken by someone else. Leave space for a short credit beneath the image.

Before printing, give each contributor a proof of their own page. Ask them to check the quantities as well as the spelling of their name. Keep the approved proof with the final file so a later reprint can be checked against the version they saw.

# Photographing objects for the club archive

Place a ruler beside each small object when taking the archive photographs. It gives the person viewing the image a size reference, since the object may look larger or smaller on a screen. Keep the ruler in the same plane as the part being measured to avoid a misleading comparison.

Use a plain surface that contrasts with the object. Pale labels can disappear against white paper, while a shiny table can reflect the room. A sheet of matt card is usually enough. Move the card rather than the object when a fragile label is already lying flat.

Photograph the reverse as well as the front when there is writing or a maker's mark. Keep both views under the same object number. For a box containing several items, take a view of the group before photographing individual pieces so the original arrangement remains available in the record.

## Giving viewers a sense of scale

An image on a screen can make a small object look large or a large one look small. Including a ruler supplies a reference against which its dimensions can be judged. Position that reference at the same depth as the surface you are measuring, because a ruler closer to the camera can suggest the wrong relative size.

Save the original images before making smaller copies for the catalogue. Use the object number in each file name and add a view description such as front, reverse, or group. Record any photograph that could not be taken and why, rather than leaving a gap that another volunteer will have to investigate later.

# What a temporary download link does

A temporary download link works until its expiry time. After that time, the same address will no longer open the file, even if it remains in your email. Ask the sender for a new link when that happens; repeatedly opening the expired address will not renew it.

The expiry applies to access through the link. A copy you have already downloaded stays wherever you saved it. Your browser may place it in Downloads or ask you to choose a folder. If you need the file later, check that the download finished before closing the page.

Some links also require you to sign in. Use the account the sender invited, since being signed in with another address can produce an access message while the link itself is still valid. If the invitation went to a shared mailbox, ask the sender which account has permission before forwarding it to another colleague.

The time limit is what makes the link temporary. Once its expiry has passed, the address in the message stops providing access to the file. Returning to that old address does not reset the deadline. The sender needs to issue another link if you still require access after the first one has expired.

Before sending a file on, check who is allowed to receive it. A link that opens for you may rely on your signed-in account and fail for the next person. The sender can confirm whether additional recipients should receive individual invitations or a shared-access link.

If the downloaded file will not open, tell the sender its file name and the application you used. A damaged download and an expired link need different responses, so include the message shown on your screen when asking for help.

# Reading a metered water bill

The number on a water meter is a running total, not the amount used since the last bill. The supplier subtracts the earlier reading from the later one to calculate the volume used between those dates. Check the reading dates before comparing one bill with another, because billing periods can have different lengths.

A bill may use an estimated reading if the supplier could not obtain an actual one. Compare the printed figure with the meter and send a dated photograph if you think the estimate is wrong. Keep the original bill until a replacement arrives so you can check which reading has changed.

The bill normally separates charges linked to consumption from fixed charges. A sewerage charge may use the metered volume with an allowance for water that does not return to the sewer. The supplier's tariff explains that allowance and any separate drainage charge.

Fixed charges continue even during a month when the property uses very little water. They can therefore make the average price per cubic metre look higher on a low-use bill. The meter itself records a cumulative total; the supplier works out consumption by taking the previous reading away from the latest one. If your tariff changed during the billing period, the bill may divide the calculated consumption between two prices. Look for the tariff dates and compare them with the dates shown on the previous statement.

Contact the supplier if the bill still seems inconsistent after checking the readings and prices. Include the account number, the reading date and the photograph. Ask for the basis of any estimate or price split so you can compare the explanation with the corrected bill when it arrives.

# When an electricity tariff changes

An electricity bill usually separates the unit rate from the standing charge. The unit rate applies to each kilowatt-hour used; the standing charge applies to each day covered by the bill. A change in either can alter the total even if your household uses the same amount of electricity.

When a tariff changes halfway through a billing period, look for two sets of dates. The supplier may use a meter reading on the change date to divide consumption between the old and new prices. Without a reading, it may estimate that division and mark the relevant figures accordingly.

Check the total number of days across both parts. Those dates should cover the billing period without a gap or an extra day. A tariff beginning on 16 May should not also be charged for 15 May, and the old tariff should finish before the new one begins.

For the consumption calculation, multiply each part's kilowatt-hours by its own unit rate. For the fixed part, multiply the days in each part by that part's standing charge. This is why the two prices introduced at the start of the bill must be checked separately: one follows the split in consumption and the other follows the split in days. Add the results before comparing them with the charges shown.

paragraphs.text: An electricity bill usually separates the unit rate from the standing charge. The unit rate applies to each kilowatt-hour used; the standing charge applies to each day covered by the bill. A change in either can alter the total even if your household uses the same amount of electricity.

When a tariff changes halfway through a billing period, look for two sets of dates. The supplier may use a meter reading on the change date to divide consumption between the old and new prices. Without a reading, it may estimate that division and mark the relevant figures accordingly.

Check the total number of days across both parts. Those dates should cover the billing period without a gap or an extra day. A tariff beginning on 16 May should not also be charged for 15 May, and the old tariff should finish before the new one begins.

For the consumption calculation, multiply each part's kilowatt-hours by its own unit rate. For the fixed part, multiply the days in each part by that part's standing charge. This is why the two prices introduced at the start of the bill must be checked separately: one follows the split in consumption and the other follows the split in days. Add the results before comparing them with the charges shown.

If the supplier revises an estimate, compare both the reading and the price allocation on the replacement bill. The overall volume may be unchanged while more of it moves into the higher-priced period. Keep the earlier statement until you understand which figures changed and why the revised total follows from them.

documents.text:
# Weighting the town travel survey

A survey weight describes how much a respondent contributes to an estimate. If younger residents respond less often than older residents, giving each response the same weight can leave younger residents underrepresented. We can increase the contribution of their responses so the age distribution of the weighted sample matches the town's population figures.

The adjustment requires reliable population counts and compatible age groups. A survey category ending at age twenty-four cannot be matched directly to a population table ending at twenty-nine. The analyst should document how the groups were reconciled and retain the original response counts beside the adjusted totals.

Weights can also be large when a small group supplies very few responses. That gives each of those respondents substantial influence over the estimate. The report should show the range of weights and explain any trimming, including which population totals were allowed to differ after trimming.

The spread of weights affects uncertainty as well as the estimate itself. A few heavily weighted responses can make a result less stable than the raw sample size suggests. Weighting lets a response count more or less towards the result; increasing the contribution from an underrepresented age group brings its weighted share into line with the population. The uncertainty calculation should use the survey design and supplied weights rather than treating the adjusted records as independent extra observations.

Matching age totals also leaves other response differences to investigate. Within the same age group, commuters who drive might be more willing to answer a travel survey than people who walk. Compare the weighted results with available independent measures and explain which characteristics were used for adjustment, so readers can judge the remaining limitations.

documents.text:
# Comparing response rates across wards

The response rate is the number of usable questionnaires divided by the number of eligible households invited. Record both counts beside the rate. Two wards can have the same percentage while supplying very different numbers of responses, which affects the precision available for later comparisons.

Eligibility needs a rule fixed before the counts are calculated. A letter returned because a property is empty can be excluded if the survey concerns occupied households. A letter that received no reply remains an invitation to an eligible household unless the team has evidence that the address was outside scope.

Check the invitation list for duplicates before publishing the denominator. If one household received two letters, the number of invitations sent differs from the number of households invited. Keep a record of how duplicates were identified, particularly when flats share a building address.

Suppose one ward returns eighty usable questionnaires from two hundred eligible households, while another returns forty from one hundred. Both response rates are forty percent. The repeated percentage does not make the two samples interchangeable: the first ward contributes twice as many responses, so a separate estimate based on that sample will generally have different uncertainty. The comparison depends on the questionnaire and sampling design as well as the count.

Report the two counts and the percentage together, using the same eligibility definition for every ward. If fieldwork found duplicate addresses or empty properties after the initial mailing, explain those changes alongside the final denominator. That allows another analyst to reproduce the calculation and see whether an apparent difference arose from participation or from the way the invitation list was cleaned.

# Preparing photographs for the club newsletter

Keep the original photograph and make a separate copy for the newsletter. A smaller copy makes the email attachment easier to send while leaving the full-resolution image available for printing. Name the newsletter copy with the issue month so it can be distinguished from the original file.

Before resizing, check that the editor has permission to publish the image and the correct credit. If the photograph shows an event, supply its date and a short description of what is happening. The editor may recognize the people but still need those details when writing the caption.

Crop only after choosing where the picture will sit on the page. A wide photograph can lose its subject when fitted into a narrow column. Send the editor the uncropped image as well if you are unsure which view works best with the layout.

Export the newsletter image at the dimensions requested by the editor and open the exported file once to check it. The full-resolution original stays available for print because the smaller file is a separate copy; the reduced version is easier to attach to an email. Add the credit and caption to the message rather than relying on a file name to carry all that information. If several photographs belong together, identify their order in the message.

Ask for the page proof when the caption contains names or event results. Check the spelling against the list supplied by the organizer, and tell the editor about any correction before the mailing is scheduled. Keep the sent message with the issue files so another volunteer can trace the credit if the photograph is reused.

# Making a large-print newsletter

Prepare the ordinary and large-print editions from the same approved text. Separate source documents can drift apart when a date or telephone number changes. Keep the issue's article text in one place and apply the layout for each edition when preparing the pages.

Ask recipients about their preferred print size and page format before settling the large-print design. A larger type size changes line lengths and can move a caption away from its photograph. Check headings, contact details and the order of articles after the layout has changed.

Some illustrations will need an alternative treatment. A timetable photographed from a noticeboard may become unreadable when enlarged. Request the original timetable or re-enter the information in a table that can use the edition's normal type size. Have someone check the dates and times against the source.

When a correction arrives, change the approved source text first and regenerate both editions. Then check the corrected item in each finished PDF. Using one source prevents the words from diverging; checking both outputs catches different layout failures, such as a telephone number breaking across lines in only one edition. Record the correction date with the issue so another volunteer can identify the latest files.

Print a sample from the large-print PDF at its intended page size. A printer option that shrinks pages to fit can undo the type-size choice. Send the approved PDFs to the person handling distribution and label each file with the issue month and edition. Keep the approved source text alongside them for the next correction.

paragraphs.text: Prepare the ordinary and large-print editions from the same approved text. Separate source documents can drift apart when a date or telephone number changes. Keep the issue's article text in one place and apply the layout for each edition when preparing the pages.

Ask recipients about their preferred print size and page format before settling the large-print design. A larger type size changes line lengths and can move a caption away from its photograph. Check headings, contact details and the order of articles after the layout has changed.

Some illustrations will need an alternative treatment. A timetable photographed from a noticeboard may become unreadable when enlarged. Request the original timetable or re-enter the information in a table that can use the edition's normal type size. Have someone check the dates and times against the source.

When a correction arrives, change the approved source text first and regenerate both editions. Then check the corrected item in each finished PDF. Using one source prevents the words from diverging; checking both outputs catches different layout failures, such as a telephone number breaking across lines in only one edition. Record the correction date with the issue so another volunteer can identify the latest files.

Print a sample from the large-print PDF at its intended page size. A printer option that shrinks pages to fit can undo the type-size choice. Send the approved PDFs to the person handling distribution and label each file with the issue month and edition. Keep the approved source text alongside them for the next correction.
